spinach.name: Spinach

sections.whatItOffers: Spinach is a leafy green that cooks down to a small, soft portion with folate, magnesium and vitamin A, and some plant iron.
sections.howToEatIt: Wilt it into soups, stews, omelettes or pasta, or stir it through warm lentils. Squeeze lemon over it or add a piece of orange to the meal: vitamin C helps your body absorb the iron.
sections.cycleRelevance: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because menstrual blood loss increases iron losses (NIH ODS). Spinach adds plant iron, which is absorbed less readily than iron from meat; vitamin C eaten with it helps. If your periods are heavy, it is worth talking to a health professional.

source.usdaDescription: Spinach, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
source.whyThisRecord: USDA has no cooked-spinach Foundation record (only raw baby and mature); the SR Legacy cooked record is the current cooked one and matches the way spinach is usually eaten and the existing catalogue wording.

keyNutrients.name: Vitamin K
keyNutrients.referenceNote: Adequate intake for women 19 and over is 90 µg; shown as an amount only. See the note on blood thinners.

cautions.text: Spinach is high in oxalate. If you have had calcium oxalate kidney stones, ask a health professional how much to eat.
cautions.source: NIDDK, Eating, Diet & Nutrition for Kidney Stones (lists spinach among foods to avoid after calcium oxalate stones)

cautions.text: Spinach is high in vitamin K. If you take warfarin or a similar blood thinner, keep your intake steady and tell your clinician.
cautions.source: NIH ODS Vitamin K (interaction with warfarin and other anticoagulants)

spinach.evidence: Iron requirement, menstrual loss and absorption: NIH ODS Iron. No spinach-specific cycle trial was used.

green-lentil.name: Lentils

sections.whatItOffers: Lentils are a filling, budget-friendly pulse with protein, fibre, folate and iron in one bowl.
sections.howToEatIt: Simmer into soups and dals, cool for salads, or fold into grain bowls. Serve with something rich in vitamin C, such as peppers, tomatoes or citrus: beans contain phytate, which makes minerals harder to absorb, and vitamin C works the other way.
sections.cycleRelevance: Like spinach, lentils add plant iron (see Spinach for why iron matters to people who menstruate), and they are also a source of folate, a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS).

source.usdaDescription: Lentils, mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt
source.whyThisRecord: USDA has only a dry lentil Foundation record; the SR Legacy cooked record is the cooked one, and it has household measures.

green-lentil.evidence: Iron absorption and folate intake statements: NIH ODS Iron and Folate. No lentil-specific cycle trial was used.

pumpkin-seeds.name: Pumpkin seeds

sections.whatItOffers: Pumpkin seeds (pepitas) are a crunchy, energy-dense source of magnesium, zinc, iron and plant protein.
sections.practicalServing: 1 ounce (28 g) of kernels (USDA: 1 cup = 129 g)
sections.howToEatIt: Scatter over porridge, yoghurt, soups or salads, or blend into a dressing or pesto. A little goes a long way: they are rich in fat and energy.
sections.cycleRelevance: We found no reliable evidence linking pumpkin seeds to a cycle phase or to period symptoms. They are here as one source of magnesium and zinc, as part of a varied diet.

source.usdaDescription: Seeds, pumpkin and squash seed kernels, dried
source.portion: 1 ounce (28 g) of kernels (USDA: 1 cup = 129 g)
source.whyThisRecord: The USDA record for the edible seed kernel (the hulled pepita), with an ounce household measure. The Foundation raw-pepitas record gives only a 30 g reference amount, so this record is the clearer match for the serving shown.

pumpkin-seeds.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only. No cycle-specific claim is made.

broccoli.name: Broccoli

sections.whatItOffers: Broccoli is a green vegetable with plenty of vitamin C and vitamin K, plus folate and fibre.
sections.howToEatIt: Steam, roast or stir-fry it until just tender. Serve it with beans, lentils or other plant iron foods: its vitamin C helps your body absorb the iron from them.
sections.cycleRelevance: We found no evidence tying broccoli to a particular phase. Its vitamin C helps your body absorb plant iron from the same meal (NIH ODS), a useful pairing for anyone who menstruates.

source.usdaDescription: Broccoli, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
source.whyThisRecord: The cooked record, as broccoli is usually eaten and as NIH ODS lists it (cooked, ½ cup). USDA has no cooked-broccoli Foundation record. The raw Foundation record (747447) is not mixed in: all amounts here are cooked.

keyNutrients.name: Vitamin K
keyNutrients.referenceNote: Adequate intake for women 19 and over is 90 µg; shown as an amount only. See the note on blood thinners.

cautions.text: Broccoli contains vitamin K. If you take warfarin or a similar blood thinner, keep your intake steady and tell your clinician.
cautions.source: NIH ODS Vitamin K (interaction with warfarin and other anticoagulants)

broccoli.evidence: Absorption statement: NIH ODS Vitamin C and Iron. No broccoli-specific cycle trial was used.

orange.name: Orange

sections.whatItOffers: An orange is a juicy, portable fruit that is an excellent source of vitamin C, with some folate and fibre.
sections.howToEatIt: Eat it whole or in segments, add to salads, or squeeze over cooked greens and lentils. Having one with an iron-rich plant meal helps your body absorb the iron.
sections.cycleRelevance: We found no evidence tying oranges to a particular phase. Vitamin C improves the absorption of plant iron (NIH ODS), so an orange pairs well with lentils or spinach.

source.whyThisRecord: The current Foundation record for an orange (navel, raw) with a household measure; it replaces the generic SR Legacy "all commercial varieties" record.

orange.evidence: Absorption statement: NIH ODS Vitamin C and Iron. No orange-specific cycle trial was used.
